text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- The new chief executive of vehicle maker Volvo, Leif Johansson, must increase the company's pace. The company's car unit is the biggest problem facing Johansson who is moving across from Electrolux.

- Sweden's central bank, the Riksbank, leaves its key interest rate, the repo rate, unchanged at 4.10 percent at its weekly operation. But bank governor Urban Backstrom says there is room for faster growth in Gross Domestic Product.

- Transport company ASG reported that its profits in 1996 slumped. The company said the reasons for the drop which cut profits almost in half were problems with computers and with the administrative system in the company's European Road Transport sector.

- Defence Minister Thage Peterson is criticised by Prime Minister Goran Persson for the way he has handled the proposed closure by vehicle group Volvo of some of its works at Arboga. Persson did not appreciate comments by Peterson about a possible military campaign against the government.

- Head of Volvo AB, Soren Gyll, who is retiring in April, will get a very valuable golden handshake, receiving 70 percent of his wages until the age of 65. He is now 56. This year he will receive his full salary then 70 percent a year until he is 65. After that he will receive 50 percent.

- Swedish appliance giant Electrolux is reported to have placed a bid on South Africa's white goods company Defy which is owned by investment company Malbak. Defy, with 2,269 staff, has about a third of the South African white goods market. The bid from Electrolux could be in the range of 320-480 million crowns.

- Thomas Franzen, director of the National Debt Office, warns that politicians should not be making commitment now for a 1998 budget surpplus as if the surplus already exists. Prime Minister Goran Persson's promise last week of a 10 billion crown surplus in 1998 caused interest rates to rise and the crown to weaken.

- Twenty-seven of the most influential business leaders in the southern Sweden region have signed a document to be made public today which identifies central goals for future development. Among the concrete proposals in the Scania Manifesto are the construction of a tunnel or bridge between Helsingborg, Sweden and Helsingor, Denmark.
